content:
<Rep. Maxine Waters, Rep. Stephen F. Lynch, Rep. Bill Foster, Rep. Joyce Beatty, Rep. Rashida Tlaib, Rep. Sylvia R. Garcia, Rep. Cleo Fields>: H.R. 5402 would amend the Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) and is designed to promote the expanded use of alternative data--specifically with respect to rent, cell phone, and utility payments--in the credit reporting system. However, which such reporting is already permitted by the FCRA and is happening to a certain degree, the legislation would preempt a number of state-level consumer protections. Instead of expanding access to credit through consumer-permissioned standards or promoting better alternative data options that have emerged in recent years, like cash flow underwriting, H.R. 5402 would make it harder for consumers to not only get credit, but also get an apartment or job, which is why we oppose this anti-consumer bill.
Credit scores and credit reports are increasingly relied upon by lenders, employers, housing providers, insurers, and even law enforcement, and now serve as a critical gatekeeper to many aspects of economic opportunity. The U.S. credit reporting system is unique because it relies on consumer data for use and profit by private companies. However, it is a system riddled with errors and shortcomings, resulting in it being a perennial top concern for consumers.<SUP>3</SUP> A recent study found that almost half of consumers who participated had mistakes in their credit reports, with more than a quarter having serious errors that damaged their credit scores.<SUP>4</SUP> Moreover, in 2017, Equifax experienced a cybersecurity breach so massive that it affected approximately 148 million consumers. In addition to releasing the personally identifiable information of approximately half of all Americans, this breach also highlighted deficiencies in the credit reporting system, including the lack of an effective dispute process for consumers who find errors in their credit reports.<SUP>5</SUP>
Meanwhile, more than two decades have passed since Congress passed comprehensive reform of the consumer reporting system.<SUP>6</SUP> And many have argued for comprehensive reforms to make the system more equitable and more accountable to consumers.<SUP>7</SUP> During the Biden Administration, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) sought to hold credit bureaus accountable and improve the credit reporting process, including by seeking to eliminate the inclusion of misleading medical debt in consumers' credit files.<SUP>8</SUP> Committee Democrats convened hearings with the major credit bureaus and advanced a number of bills to overhaul the credit reporting system, including several to promote the use of alternative data.<SUP>9</SUP>
In contrast, the Trump Administration and Congressional Republicans have prioritized efforts to undermine the CFPB, including by slashing the agency's budget by nearly half, attempting to fire most of the staff, and halting the supervision of large credit bureaus and other major financial companies for compliance with consumer protection laws. Some estimates show that with all their CFPB rollbacks, in just a year, the Trump Administration has already cost consumers at least $19 billion.<SUP>10</SUP> Additionally, the Trump Administration recently made it harder for consumers to file complaints through CFPB's complaint database, particularly regarding problems they have with consumer credit reporting.<SUP>11</SUP> They did this after such consumer complaints exploded under their watch. In 2020, the CFPB handled about 542,300 complaints, with more than 58% of those complaints regarding credit and consumer reporting representing the most complaints received about any consumer product or service during that time.<SUP>12</SUP> Five years later, in 2025, the CFPB received a record 6.6 million complaints as Trump shutdown the CFPB, while the vast majority--5.8 million of those complaints (88%)--were about credit reporting.<SUP>13</SUP>
The House previously passed a version of this measure eight years ago in the 115th Congress.<SUP>14</SUP> Back then, the Committee was seeking to promote the use of alternative data-- like the reporting of rental, cell phone, and utility bill payments--but a lot has changed since then. Back then, even in a Republican Administration, we had a functioning CFPB and didn't see the kind of radical and unlawful shutdown of the agency that we've seen in Trump's second term. Furthermore, alternative data has been increasingly reported and included in various types of credit scores. The Committee later held a hearing on a revised Democratic draft that would address consumer advocate concerns,<SUP>15</SUP> including not preempting state protections and empowering consumers to opt-in to sharing such data. Negating state protections, as H.R. 5402 would do, after undermining the operations of the Federal agency with authority to supervise and enforce FCRA, would leave consumers worse off.
At a time when consumer data is increasingly used throughout the economy, an opt-in provision would give consumers more control over their own data, an approach that gained bipartisan support when this Congress curbed abusive trigger leads in 2025.<SUP>16</SUP> To that end, Rep. Janelle Bynum (D-OR) offered an amendment to add an opt-in requirement to allow consumers to decide if their information is shared with credit bureaus. This amendment also would eliminate the bill's sweeping preemption of protections for consumers available at the state level. Ranking Member Waters (D-CA) offered an amendment to restore CFPB funding and staffing for purposes of supervising and enforcing to ensure adequate oversight of credit bureaus and the credit reporting system. Unfortunately, Republicans rejected both amendments and instead further harmed consumers by removing a provision that would have allowed a consumer to opt-out from having their information shared with credit bureaus.
Consumer groups are strongly opposed to H.R. 5402 and have warned the bill would reduce a consumer's control over their own data; override state law protections for renters from tenant screening abuses; make it harder for consumers to obtain rental housing; and undermine other state consumer protections.<SUP>17</SUP> They also note there is a range of better alternatives to expand the use of alternative data, like cash flow underwriting.<SUP>18</SUP> Specifically, 70 consumer, housing, civil rights, utility rights, and advocacy groups are opposed to H.R. 5402, including the following national organizations: National Consumer Law Center (on behalf of its low-income clients), 20/20 Vision, Accountable.US/ Accountable.NOW, Americans for Financial Reform (AFR), Center for Digital Democracy, Center for Economic Justice, Consumer Action, Consumer Federation of America, Consumer Reports, National Association of Consumer Advocates, National Association of State Utility Consumer Advocates (NASUCA), National Consumers League, National Fair Housing Alliance, National Housing Law Project, and Public Citizen. The bill was also opposed by the following state and local organizations: Center for Economic Integrity (AZ), William E. Morris Institute for Justice (AZ), Arkansas Community Organizations, Community Legal Services in East Palo Alto (CA), Center for Accessible Technology (CA), Disability Rights California, Housing and Economic Rights Advocates (CA), The Academy of Financial Education (CA), TURN-The Utility Reform Network (CA), Watsonville Law Center (CA), Western Center on Law & Poverty (CA), Colorado Poverty Law Project, Connecticut Legal Services, Inc., Legal Aid DC, Jacksonville Area Legal Aid (FL), Florida Legal Services, Inc., Georgia Watch, Legal Action Chicago, Citizens Action Coalition of IN, Legal Key Partnership for Health and Justice (MA/RI), Coastal Enterprises, Inc. (ME), Maine People's Alliance, Economic Action Maryland Fund, Low- Income Energy Affordability Network (LEAN)(MA), Public Justice Center (MD), Michigan Poverty Law Program, Housing Justice Center (MN), Legal Aid Center of Southern Nevada, Nevada Coalition of Legal Service Providers, Legal Services of New Jersey, New Jersey Appleseed Public Interest Law Center, New Jersey Citizen Action, New Jersey Institute for Social Justice, New Economy Project (NY), New Yorkers for Responsible Lending, Western New York Law Center, Inc., Legal Aid Society of Southwest Ohio, Oregon Consumer Justice, Oregon Consumer League, HELP: MLP (PA), Philadelphia Solar Energy Association, Pennsylvania Utility Law Project (on behalf of its low- income clients), Community Legal Services of Philadelphia, George Wiley Center (RI), South Carolina Appleseed Legal Justice Center, Texas Utility Law Project, Texas Appleseed, Legal Aid Justice Center (VA), Vermont Legal Aid, Virginia Citizens Consumer Council, Virginia Organizing, Hopelink (WA), Byrd Barr Place (WA), El Centro de la Raza (WA), and Washington State Community Action Partnership.<SUP>19</SUP>
For these reasons, we oppose H.R. 5402.
Sincerely,
Maxine Waters,
Ranking Member.
Stephen F. Lynch,
Bill Foster,
Joyce Beatty,
Rashida Tlaib,
Sylvia R. Garcia,
Cleo Fields,
Members of Congress.
